challenges.title: Recall checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Without reopening the lesson, explain Curriculum Companion: Why Every Week Exists in your own words. Include the problem it solves, the core mechanism, and one boundary or failure.
challenges.hint: Use “Week 1 — Repository contract” as a cue, then close the lesson again.

challenges.title: Prediction checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Choose one example or source file from this mission. Predict its behavior for a normal input and a changed or invalid input before running or revealing the reference. Explain the rule separating the outcomes.
challenges.hint: Change one condition at a time so the result teaches a rule.

challenges.title: Build and prove checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Implement, debug, or adapt the mission exercise yourself. Record the acceptance criterion, command or interaction used to verify it, failure evidence, and one tradeoff. Do not paste the reference solution.
challenges.hint: A passing check, measured result, focused diff, or reproducible demo is stronger than ‘done.’

files.content:
# Curriculum Companion: Why Every Week Exists

The curriculum checklist tells you what to deliver. This companion explains
the engineering problem each week is designed to solve, what “good” looks like,
and what to discuss in a review. Read the matching section at the beginning and
end of each week.

## Week 1 — Repository contract

### Why this matters

Professional code is changed by more than the machine on which it was written.
A repository therefore needs a contract: supported tool versions, repeatable
setup, consistent formatting, automated checks, and a clear contribution path.
Without it, “works on my machine” becomes hidden state that teammates and CI
cannot reproduce.

The walking skeleton should cross every major boundary early: browser, API,
database, and deployment. A tiny end-to-end path exposes integration mistakes
while they are cheap. Building every layer separately for weeks delays the
first honest feedback until the architecture is expensive to change.

### Concrete example

A page that displays one board name loaded through the real API and real
database is more valuable than ten polished static screens. It proves routing,
configuration, serialization, network policy, migrations, and deployment can
work together.

### Common traps

- CI runs a different command from developers.
- Setup requires an undocumented global tool or manual database click.
- Formatting rewrites deliberately generated/vendor content.
- One enormous “initial project” commit hides decision history.
- Secrets are committed because `.env` was created before ignore rules.
- Architecture is chosen before product boundaries and constraints are known.

### Review questions

- Can a clean machine reproduce the same result?
- Does failure output tell a newcomer what action to take?
- Which decision is expensive to reverse, and where is it recorded?
- What useful end-to-end behavior exists after this week?

## Week 2 — Testing strategy

### Why this matters

Testing is risk management, not a contest for the most assertions. Different
boundaries catch different failures. Unit tests quickly protect domain rules;
database integration tests prove mappings and constraints; API tests exercise
middleware and serialization; component tests protect user-visible behavior;
browser tests prove a small number of critical journeys work together.

Writing the strategy early prevents two extremes: everything mocked at the
unit level, or every tiny rule tested through a slow browser.

### Concrete example

For “only board members can read a card”:

- unit test the authorization rule's decisions;
- API integration test that identity, route binding, and repository combine;
- browser test one representative unauthorized journey.

The same risk is viewed at increasing cost and confidence, not duplicated
mechanically at every layer.

### Common traps

- A mock returns the value the implementation expects, proving nothing.
- Tests pass individually but share state and fail as a suite.
- Arbitrary sleeps hide missing synchronization.
- Teardown starts cleanup without awaiting it, leaving open handles.
- Snapshot files replace meaningful behavioral assertions.
- Coverage rises while important authorization and failure paths remain absent.

### Review questions

- What real defect would each test catch?
- Why is this the cheapest sufficient boundary?
- Can tests run in any order and in parallel?
- What failure remains intentionally untested, and why?

## Week 3 — Relational data

### Why this matters

Application validation improves error messages, but only database constraints
protect data from every writer, race, migration, and bug. A relational model
turns business truths into durable structure: ownership, uniqueness,
relationships, valid ranges, and atomic transitions.

Indexes are not decoration. They trade write/storage cost for specific read
paths. Learn to start from a query, inspect its plan with representative data,
and justify an index by evidence.

### Concrete example

Moving a card may update its column, position, board version, and activity
record. If those writes partially succeed, clients observe a state that never
represented a valid user action. A transaction makes the invariant—not the
individual SQL statement—the atomic unit.

### Common traps

- Use an ORM without understanding emitted queries.
- Store ordering as values that become expensive to renumber without a plan.
- Add indexes to every column and slow writes unnecessarily.
- Test against an in-memory substitute with different SQL semantics.
- Add a required column in one breaking migration during a rolling deployment.
- Trust TypeScript/C# nullability to protect stored data.

### Review questions

- Which invalid states does the database itself reject?
- Which query does every index support?
- What can race, and where is the transaction boundary?
- How can the previous application version coexist with the migration?

## Week 4 — HTTP API contract

### Why this matters

An API is a promise between independently changing systems. Clear resources,
status codes, schemas, failure shapes, pagination, idempotency, and concurrency
behavior let clients operate without reading server internals.

Runtime validation remains required even with TypeScript or generated clients:
the network transports bytes, and callers can be old, buggy, or hostile.

### Concrete example

Creating a card can succeed while its response is lost. The client retries the
same idempotency key and must receive the original outcome. Editing a stale card
is different: the server should surface a version conflict rather than silently
overwriting newer work.

### Common traps

- Return `200` for every outcome and encode failure only in text.
- Use offset pagination on a changing activity feed.
- Generate OpenAPI after implementation but never verify it matches behavior.
- Retry all errors, multiplying load during an outage.
- Return raw exceptions and internal stack traces.
- Authorize the route but not the requested resource.

### Review questions

- Can another developer build a client from the contract alone?
- Which commands are safe to retry, and why?
- What does a stale update receive?
- How are old clients protected when the contract evolves?

## Week 5 — Production React client

### Why this matters

Concept demos can use one HTML file, but professional React work involves
modules, build tooling, types, routing, data boundaries, testing, and deployment.
The client must also represent every important async state, not only the happy
path shown on a fast local machine.

Accessibility is interaction correctness. Keyboard focus, semantics, labels,
and announcements should be designed with component behavior, not applied as a
final audit.

### Concrete example

An optimistic card move should render immediately, retain a stable client
operation ID, disable or reconcile conflicting actions, roll back on rejection,
and announce failure accessibly. The server remains authoritative; optimistic
UI is a temporary hypothesis with an explicit resolution path.

### Common traps

- Copy pure logic into HTML instead of importing one source.
- Store data that can be derived, creating synchronization bugs.
- Use effects to calculate values during rendering.
- Handle loading but omit empty, unauthorized, stale, offline, and retry states.
- Optimize with memoization before measuring a problem.
- Test component implementation details instead of user behavior.

### Review questions

- Who owns each category of state?
- What happens on slow, failed, stale, and repeated responses?
- Can the journey be completed with a keyboard?
- What measurement justified the performance change?

## Week 6 — Authentication and authorization

### Why this matters

Authentication answers “who is this?” Authorization answers “may this identity
perform this operation on this resource?” A valid session must never imply
access to every object. Many serious application failures come from checking
the first question and forgetting the second.

Security work begins with assets and trust boundaries, then adds layered
controls and abuse tests. A feature is not secure merely because password
hashing exists.

### Concrete example

User A changes `/boards/A` to `/boards/B`, where B is a real private board. A
safe service applies membership filtering before revealing whether B exists,
and the same rule protects list queries, card endpoints, activity history, and
realtime subscriptions.

### Common traps

- Trust an owner/user ID from the request body.
- Put sessions in logs or browser storage vulnerable to the chosen threat model.
- Return different login messages that enumerate accounts.
- Protect HTTP reads but forget WebSocket subscription authorization.
- Apply CORS as if it were an authorization mechanism.
- Write custom cryptography instead of using maintained platform primitives.

### Review questions

- What assets and attacker-controlled inputs exist?
- Where is resource authorization enforced and tested?
- What happens after logout, expiration, theft, or password change?
- Which residual risks are accepted for version 1?

## Week 7 — Asynchrony and resilience

### Why this matters

Distributed operations can be delayed, duplicated, reordered, partially
completed, or abandoned. Resilience comes from bounded resources, explicit
delivery semantics, idempotent effects, cancellation, timeouts, and visible
failure—not from wrapping every call in retries.

Queues move work in time. They also create backlog, redelivery, shutdown, and
poison-message problems that synchronous code did not have.

### Concrete example

A notification worker receives the same activity event twice after restarting.
An idempotent consumer records a stable event/message identity and produces one
durable notification effect. If work repeatedly fails, operators can see and
reprocess or discard it deliberately.

### Common traps

- Fire-and-forget work that disappears when the process exits.
- Unbounded queues that turn traffic spikes into memory exhaustion.
- Retry permanent validation failures.
- Ignore cancellation after the client no longer needs the work.
- Claim exactly-once delivery when only processing attempts are counted.
- Shut down the process without draining or safely returning leased work.

### Review questions

- What is bounded, and what happens when the bound is reached?
- Which effects are safe under duplicate delivery?
- Where do timeouts end and cancellation propagate?
- How is failed work discovered and recovered?

## Week 8 — Observability

### Why this matters

An unobservable system may appear healthy while users fail. Logs, metrics,
traces, and health checks answer different questions. The aim is not maximum
telemetry volume; it is the ability to detect impact, locate a cause, and
verify recovery without exposing sensitive data.

### Concrete example

An alert shows elevated p95 card-move latency. A trace separates API time from
database lock waiting; structured logs connect a request ID to the board and
conflict outcome; a metric shows queue depth is normal. Evidence narrows the
problem before code changes begin.

### Common traps

- Free-form logs with IDs embedded only in sentences.
- High-cardinality user/request IDs used as metric labels.
- Health endpoint always returns 200 without checking readiness.
- Log entire request objects and leak credentials.
- Alert on internal noise rather than user impact.
- Add instrumentation that changes timing enough to hide the race.

### Review questions

- What signal detects user impact first?
- Can one request be followed across boundaries?
- Which secrets were seeded to prove redaction?
- What does readiness mean for this application?

## Week 9 — Containers and deployment

### Why this matters

Deployment is part of software behavior. Reproducible builds, explicit
configuration, safe migrations, health checks, and rollback reduce the gap
between code that passes locally and code that can operate elsewhere.

Containers package a process and its runtime dependencies; they do not remove
the need to understand networking, storage, identity, resource limits, or
application shutdown.

### Concrete example

A new API version expects a column that the old database lacks. Safe delivery
orders an additive migration before the new code, allows old and new versions
to coexist, backfills data, and contracts the schema only after old code is
gone.

### Common traps

- Bake secrets into images or compose files.
- Run as root by default.
- Use `latest` without recording what was deployed.
- Make images enormous by copying build caches and source unnecessarily.
- Couple schema migration irreversibly to application startup.
- Document a rollback that fails because the database already changed.

### Review questions

- Is the artifact identical across environments?
- How is configuration supplied and validated?
- Can old and new versions coexist during rollout?
- What was actually tested about rollback or roll-forward?

## Week 10 — Debugging and maintenance

### Why this matters

Most professional work changes existing systems under imperfect information.
Systematic debugging separates evidence from intuition, creates a reliable
reproduction, discriminates hypotheses, and protects the fix with a regression
test. Maintenance also requires evolving contracts without coordinated instant
updates of every client and data row.

### Concrete example

A WebSocket integration test passes but never lets the process exit. The test
assertions are green, yet an open socket or unawaited server close keeps an
active handle alive. Inspecting lifecycle ownership reveals the root cause;
forcing process exit would only hide it.

### Common traps

- Change several suspected causes simultaneously.
- Fix the symptom with a timeout or retry.
- Write the regression test after the fix and never see it fail.
- Profile unrealistic data and optimize the wrong path.
- Rename a field in server, client, and database as one atomic deployment.
- Blame an individual instead of improving feedback and system safeguards.

### Review questions

- Which observation rules out each rejected hypothesis?
- Did the regression test fail for the intended reason?
- Is the fix smaller than the investigation?
- What will detect recurrence sooner?

## Week 11 — Scale and tradeoffs

### Why this matters

System design is disciplined reasoning under assumptions, not naming the most
technologies. Estimate traffic, storage, concurrency, and quality targets;
identify the first likely constraint; then choose the least complex design
that satisfies current needs and has an evolution path.

### Concrete example

Ten thousand mostly idle WebSocket connections stress memory and connection
limits differently from ten thousand card moves per second. “Ten thousand
users” is not sufficient input. State concurrent connections, messages per
second, message size, fan-out, and reconnection behavior.

### Common traps

- Start with microservices before identifying boundaries.
- Call a cache a solution without defining invalidation and stale behavior.
- State enormous scale without unit arithmetic.
- Ignore hot boards that dominate fan-out.
- Assume a queue makes work reliable automatically.
- Design only the happy path and omit recovery.

### Review questions

- Which assumption most affects the design?
- What saturates first, supported by what evidence?
- What consistency does the user actually need?
- What complexity is intentionally deferred?

## Week 12 — Portfolio conversion

### Why this matters

Good work is not automatically legible to a recruiter or interviewer. A
portfolio must quickly establish the problem, your ownership, a runnable/demo
path, technical depth, evidence, and honest limitations. Communication is part
of engineering because decisions and operations must survive beyond the author.

### Concrete example

“Built a task app” says little. A case study that shows idempotent offline
mutations, authorization abuse tests, a diagnosed concurrency defect, measured
p95 latency, and a rehearsed rollback demonstrates transferable engineering.

### Common traps

- Lead with technology badges instead of the user problem.
- Report test counts without describing risks covered.
- Invent users or business impact for a personal project.
- Hide limitations and appear unable to evaluate your own system.
- Present only the final code and erase iteration evidence.
- Give a 30-minute answer when asked for a two-minute overview.

### Review questions

- Can a stranger understand the value in five minutes?
- Are all claims inspectable and reproducible?
- Can you explain three meaningful tradeoffs?
- What did failure teach you that a tutorial would not?

## How to use this companion

At the start of a week, choose one common trap you are most likely to fall into
and write how you will detect it. At the end, answer the four review questions
without notes. Any answer that remains vague becomes a concrete issue or
experiment for the next week.
